summary: Defines how an IKEv2 client and gateway can resume a previous session with fewer round trips and less cryptographic work. This helps remote-access VPNs where EAP authentication is expensive or a gateway fails over. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If you already showed your badge this morning, a guard can wave you in quickly when you come back instead of checking everything again. This lets a VPN session restart fast.

questions: how does ikev2 session resumption work
how to reconnect a vpn without full authentication
ticket by value vs ticket by reference ikev2
subtitle: How an IKEv2 client can quickly resume a dropped VPN session with a ticket instead of authenticating all over again.

tldr.problem: Re-establishing an IKEv2 session after a failure takes many round trips and cryptographic work, especially with EAP authentication and a gateway that must bring back many clients at once.
tldr.mechanism: The gateway gives the client an opaque ticket holding or pointing to the old IKE state. After a break, the client sends the ticket in a new IKE_SESSION_RESUME exchange, and fresh keys are derived from the old SK_d and new nonces using only symmetric cryptography.
tldr.outcome: A session can resume with less overhead and no user interaction. Tickets are single use, short lived and tied to one IKE SA, and the RFC covers failure recovery to the same gateway only.

today: RFC 5723 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers resuming to the same gateway only; failover between gateways is listed as a non-goal.

sections.title: The Problem and the Ticket Idea
sections.content:
IKEv2 has computational and communication overhead. In remote access, the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) adds more round trips. After a failure, a VPN gateway may have to rebuild a large number of security associations at once, and users may have to re-authenticate by hand.

RFC 5723 lets a client resume using a ticket, an opaque data structure created by the responder. There are two flavours. With ticket by reference, the gateway keeps the state and gives the client an opaque reference to it. With ticket by value, the gateway encrypts and integrity-protects its state under a key only it knows and hands that to the client. The client behaves the same in both cases. The approach is modelled on TLS session resumption (RFC 5077).

Goals are symmetric-only cryptography, cryptographic agility and no harm to IKEv2 security. Non-goals are failover between gateways, load balancing and detecting when resumption is needed.
sections.eli5: When you first get in, the gateway gives you a sealed envelope. Next time, you hand it back and it remembers you without asking all the questions again.

sections.title: Usage Scenarios
sections.content:
Two settings are envisioned: a remote access client reaching a gateway through an IPsec tunnel, and two servers protecting a client-server protocol with transport or tunnel mode.

The RFC lists situations where resumption helps. A client that briefly loses connectivity and times out through dead peer detection can reconnect with less overhead and no user interaction. When many clients lose connectivity together, resumption reduces the load spike on the gateway when they all return. A laptop put into stand-by could resume too, although the RFC notes that policy may often disallow user-level resumption, and the client must destroy its ticket when the user explicitly logs out.
sections.eli5: It helps when your connection drops for a moment, when a whole crowd reconnects at once, or when you close your laptop and open it again.

sections.title: Getting and Using a Ticket
sections.content:
A client MAY request a ticket by including a TICKET_REQUEST notification in the first IKE_AUTH request. It can also ask during rekeying of the IKE SA (when the client starts it), in an Informational exchange at any time, or in the IKE_AUTH that follows a resumption. The responder answers with TICKET_LT_OPAQUE carrying the ticket, TICKET_NACK to refuse, or TICKET_ACK if it cannot grant one right now, for example due to packet size limits. The normal IKE response is always sent as well.

To resume, the client sends a new exchange type, IKE_SESSION_RESUME (value 38), containing a nonce Ni and a TICKET_OPAQUE notification. It acts like IKE_SA_INIT, and MUST be followed by IKE_AUTH. The initiator sets SPIi to a new unique value and SPIr to 0. If the gateway accepts, it replies with its nonce Nr. If it rejects the ticket it sends an unprotected TICKET_NACK and the client starts a regular IKE exchange.

The client may resume from any IP address and port, and NAT traversal status is determined anew. Tickets are one-time use: a client MUST NOT reuse one, and a reused ticket SHOULD be rejected. A client MUST NOT present a ticket it knows has expired, but MAY choose a regular exchange anyway.
sections.eli5: You ask for an envelope when you sign in. If the connection drops, you show it to the gateway. If it is not accepted, you simply do the long check-in again.

sections.title: Authenticating the Resumed Session
sections.content:
After IKE_SESSION_RESUME, the client MUST run an IKE_AUTH exchange. The AUTH payload is computed like pre-shared secret authentication, as AUTH = prf(SK_px, message octets), using SK_pi for the initiator and SK_pr for the responder from the newly generated keys.

The IDi in IKE_AUTH MUST match the value in the ticket. No CERT payload is allowed, so a new IDr cannot be negotiated, and the IDr sent MUST also match the ticket. A client will typically ask for a new ticket in this same IKE_AUTH so it can resume again after a second failure. When the responder accepts a ticket for an IKE SA that is still active, it SHOULD silently delete the old SA without a DELETE exchange, which also deletes its Child SAs.
sections.eli5: Even with the envelope, you still prove it is really you using a secret only the two of you share, and your name has to match the one inside.

sections.title: State and Keys After Resumption
sections.content:
Section 5 has a table of what happens to each piece of IKE and IPsec state. The identities, authentication method, certificates when needed, and IKE SA algorithms come from the ticket. NAT detection status, SPIs and MOBIKE support come from the new exchange. Message IDs reset to 0 and the window size resets to 1. Child SAs are created in a new exchange, and the internal IP address and other configuration payload information are not resumed, though the client can ask for its earlier address.

Keys are refreshed using the old SK_d from the ticket and both nonces: SKEYSEED = prf(SK_d_old, "Resumption" | Ni | Nr). The usual keys SK_d, SK_ai, SK_ar, SK_ei, SK_er, SK_pi and SK_pr are then derived with prf+ from SKEYSEED, the nonces and the new SPIs. The literal string is 10 ASCII characters with no NULL terminator.
sections.eli5: The old secret is stirred together with fresh random numbers from both sides, so the new session gets brand new keys.

sections.title: Ticket Contents and Lifecycle
sections.content:
A ticket by value MUST be integrity protected and encrypted, and MUST contain all state marked as coming from the ticket. It MUST include a protected absolute expiration time and a key identity field, so keys and algorithms can be changed. A ticket by reference need not be encrypted, but access to the state store MUST be protected, and integrity protection is RECOMMENDED to avoid problems such as SQL injection. The exact ticket format is left to implementers; Appendix A gives examples for both kinds.

Each ticket belongs to a single IKE SA. The client MUST delete it when the IKE SA is deleted or its credentials are invalidated, and rekeying invalidates it, so the client SHOULD request a new one. The ticket lifetime SHOULD be the minimum of the IKE SA lifetime and the re-authentication time, and a finite lifetime is always required. The key protecting tickets MUST live significantly longer than an IKE SA.
sections.eli5: An envelope is good for only one trip and one visit. It has an expiry date, and you throw it away when you log out.

sections.title: The Ticket Notifications
sections.content: Five new Notify Message types are defined, all with Protocol ID and SPI Size sent as 0. TICKET_LT_OPAQUE carries a four-octet Lifetime field, the number of seconds until the ticket expires as an unsigned integer in network byte order, followed by the ticket. TICKET_OPAQUE carries just the ticket with no lifetime. TICKET_REQUEST, TICKET_ACK and TICKET_NACK carry no data. IANA allocated the IKE_SESSION_RESUME exchange type and the notification values.
sections.eli5: These are the little labelled notes the two sides pass back and forth: please give me a ticket, here it is, no thanks, or later.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A stolen ticket is of no use on its own, because the thief cannot prove knowledge of the secret IKE state during IKE_AUTH. The responder MUST use strong encryption and integrity protection for ticket by value, and MUST enforce access control on reference resolution. Forging or altering a ticket fails if strong integrity protection is used.

Denial of service is a concern: floods of tickets by value burden the CPU, and floods of references force lookups, so verification and resolution should be lightweight. The regular IKEv2 cookie mechanism can handle state overflow. Recommended key practice includes secure generation, at least 128 bits of strength, no other uses, and regular changes.

Revoked tickets by value could be replayed by a misbehaving client. A gateway may keep an Invalid Ticket List, and short lifetimes (the RFC gives 1 hour as an example) mitigate the issue. Because the resumption exchange is not confidential, an observer could link repeated use of the same ticket to the same endpoints, which is why tickets are single use.
sections.eli5: A copied envelope is useless without the secret inside, but the gateway should still check envelopes quickly, change its locks often, and never let one be used twice.

messages.label: IKE_AUTH + N(TICKET_REQUEST)
messages.note: Ask for a ticket during normal setup.

items.label: TICKET_LT_OPAQUE
items.desc: Carries a lifetime in seconds and the ticket.

items.label: TICKET_REQUEST
items.desc: Client asks for a ticket; no data.

items.label: TICKET_ACK
items.desc: Cannot grant a ticket now; no data.

items.label: TICKET_NACK
items.desc: Refuses a ticket request or rejects a presented ticket; no data.

items.label: TICKET_OPAQUE
items.desc: Carries the ticket the client presents.

items.title: Ticket by value
items.text: The gateway's state, encrypted and integrity-protected under a key only the gateway knows.

items.title: Ticket by reference
items.text: An opaque reference to state kept in the gateway's own store.
